A1.justification: Both PDFs describe EDINET-Bench and the same underlying Japanese financial-report corpus. Their complete main texts, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations on three financial tasks, contamination checks, confusion matrices, and worked prediction examples.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds evaluations of further LLMs, a fine-tuned model, and classical classifiers in Table 6.

M1.justification: The benchmark construction procedure remains based on EDINET extraction, Claude 3.7 Sonnet assessment of amendment reasons, earnings-change labels, and the same industry grouping. The evaluation prompts retain their substantive instructions. Fine-tuning is introduced as a comparison baseline; expanded manual-review reporting does not establish a changed labeling algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Japanese company reports on fraud detection, earnings forecasting, industry prediction, and the company-name contamination check. The corpus collection period remains April 2014 to April 2025. The added industry training split changes experimental design within retained coverage; multilingual and agentic extensions remain future work.

E2.justification: Table 6 adds GPT-5, Kimi-K2, Llama 3.3 70B, fine-tuned Llama-3.2-1B, Random Forest, and XGBoost. Logistic regression also joins the industry-prediction comparison. The naive earnings-trend baseline disappears from the reported comparison, although its label-construction description remains.

E3.justification: v2 adds a 900-example industry training split where v1 explicitly had no training split, and introduces supervised LLM evaluation. Classical models are evaluated across all three input configurations, extending v1's Summary-only logistic setup. Industry report selection is now described as the latest fiscal year's report instead of fiscal-year-2023 reports. This reported selection change does not establish that the unchanged original score entries were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 removes the class-specific error diagnostics provided by v1's main-text and appendix confusion matrices across all three tasks, including Figures 17-18, 21-22, and 25. This substantially reduces evidence about false positives, false negatives, and industry confusions. The input-section comparisons, logistic feature analysis, contamination checks, and six worked model-response examples are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report LLM means and standard deviations over three runs and specify GPT-4o seed 0. No new confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures appear. The newly quantified manual label-check finding is an additional result, without a documented change in statistical estimation practice.

E6.justification: The seven original LLMs' Table 6 scores remain identical, but substantial new results appear: Random Forest reaches fraud ROC-AUC 0.75 with Summary input, GPT-5 reaches earnings ROC-AUC 0.65 with all sections, and XGBoost reaches industry accuracy 0.42 with tabular sections. The naive baseline's earnings ROC-AUC 0.44 and MCC -0.12 disappear, along with confusion-matrix results. Section 3.3 newly quantifies the existing manual label check as fewer than 5% unrelated fraud-labeled cases.

T1.justification: Neither version presents formal theoretical results or proofs. The task-label definitions, industry mapping, and evaluation metrics retain their mathematical substance.

C1.justification: The central benchmark contribution and claim that frontier LLMs struggle remain. v2 adds an explicit, qualified claim to be the first open accounting-fraud dataset and benchmark. Its abstract and conclusion emphasize realistic scaffolding and task-specific reasoning support more strongly, developing directions already present in v1's discussion of agentic pipelines.

C2.justification: v2 emphasizes label reliability using the fewer-than-5% manual-check finding, while removing explicit caveats about unintentional errors, undiscovered fraud among negative labels, parsing-induced false positives, and historical industry-label mismatch. These change the qualification of benchmark validity. Contamination caveats and the need for information beyond annual reports survive in revised locations; auditor-reputation bias also remains. Future work expands the discussion of multilingual evaluation and specific agent tools.

D1.justification: v2 removes v1's scikit-learn/default-hyperparameter specification, parsed-input examples, source report identifiers in case captions, and documentation of excluding companies with changed industry labels. It adds a GPT-5 model identifier and an explicit EDINET-Corpus release commitment. Core prompts, inference parameters, cost information, and dataset/code links remain. Omission of the industry filter description does not establish that filtering stopped.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning through a new financial-benchmark comparison table, discussion of FinanceMATH and AuditBench, and connections to Humanity's Last Exam, SWE-Bench variants, and WebArena. It strengthens the claimed distinction around expert-level reasoning and adds discussion of contamination-detection approaches. Several earlier references, including BloombergGPT, PIXIU, and FinGPT, disappear.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around benchmark difficulty and expert reasoning. Evaluation setup is reorganized, the standalone Limitations section is removed with some content redistributed, and Future Work, Reproducibility Statement, and LLM Usage sections are added. Appendices are substantially condensed and reorganized, beyond changes caused by added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adopts the ICLR layout, redraws Figure 1, replaces the TSV-example table with a benchmark-comparison table, and restructures Table 6 into model groups. Confusion matrices and parsed-report figures are removed. The fraud-prediction prompt moves into the main text, retained response examples are consolidated, and the industry-mapping table is reformatted. The year-wise plots retain identical graphical content.

improvement.justification: The expanded comparisons address v1's narrow classical-baseline evaluation: Random Forest's leading fraud result and XGBoost's industry result provide more informative context for LLM performance. Quantifying the manual label check also improves the evidence presented. These gains are limited by removed error diagnostics, validity caveats, and reproducibility details. v2 additionally retains the claim that Claude 3.5 Sonnet's 0.41 industry accuracy is state of the art despite reporting XGBoost at 0.42. The broader empirical foundation supports a modest overall improvement.
